Content:
Suppose we have two point masses [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] of mass [MATH: 20\,\textrm{kg}] and [MATH: 40\,\textrm{kg},] respectively, connected by a rigid, massless rod of length [MATH: 1\,\textrm{m}], as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fc89bbb4b2e7e8053a4413f5a81b873b]

Content:
Our intuition tells us that if we place a fulcrum (i.e., a balancing point) at the midpoint between the two masses, the rod will tip down at the right end, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3942ec65acf89851b3934dedde08467d]

Content:
To balance the rod perfectly, we must move the fulcrum closer to the larger mass.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/8ca82f4e75f06d9a7db1d3718cd02562]

Content:
At what distance from the first mass ([MATH: d_1] in the picture) should the fulcrum be placed for the masses to balance perfectly?

Content:
To answer this, we must introduce the concept of a moment:

Content:
> The moment of a mass about a point [MATH: P] equals the product of the mass and its displacement from [MATH: P.]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- Loosely speaking, moment describes the amount of turning effect produced by a mass about a point (usually the tip of the fulcrum).
- For masses measured in kilograms and distances in meters, the units of a moment are [MATH: \textrm{kg}\cdot\textrm m.]
- Moment is a vector quantity. A moment is either positive (representing clockwise induced motion) or negative (for counterclockwise motion). A moment's sign (positive/clockwise or negative/counterclockwise) is determined by the direction the rod would rotate if the corresponding mass were the only mass in the system.

Content:
Let's now see how to use moments to calculate the required distance [MATH: d_1.]

Content:
The principle of moments tells us that, for the two masses to balance, the sum of the moments must equal zero.

Content:
So in our case, we have

Using the fact that the rod has length [MATH: 1\,\textrm{m},] we have

Content:
Substituting this into the first equation, we get

Content:
[MATH: 40(1-d_1) - 20d_1 = 0]

Content:
which solves to give

Content:
[MATH: d_1 = \dfrac23\,\textrm m.]

Content:
Therefore, if the fulcrum is placed at a distance of [MATH: \dfrac23\,\textrm m] from [MATH: A,] the rod would balance perfectly.

sections.normalized_html:
The moment about the origin [MATH: O] of a collection of masses [MATH: m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_n] located at [MATH: x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n] along the [MATH: x]-axis is given by

[MATH: M_O = \sum_{i=1}^n m_i x_i.]

In our case, we have

[MATH: m_{1}|= 1,|m_{2}|= 2,|m_{3}|= 3,|m_{4}|= 3,; x_{1}|= − 1,|x_{2}|= 1,|x_{3}|= 3,|x_{4}|= 5.]

We calculate the total moment of this system about the origin as follows:

[MATH: M_{O}|= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)m_{i}x_{i}; = m_{1}x_{1} + m_{2}x_{2} + m_{3}x_{3} + m_{4}x_{4}; = 1 ⋅ (− 1) + 2 ⋅ 1 + 3 ⋅ 3 + 3 ⋅ 5; = − 1 + 2 + 9 + 15; = 25]

Therefore, the total moment of the system is [MATH: 25\,\textrm{kg} \cdot \textrm{m}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we have two point masses [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] of mass [MATH: 20\,\textrm{kg}] and [MATH: 40\,\textrm{kg},] respectively, connected by a rigid, massless rod of length [MATH: 1\,\textrm{m}], as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fc89bbb4b2e7e8053a4413f5a81b873b]

Content:
Our intuition tells us that if we place a fulcrum (i.e., a balancing point) at the midpoint between the two masses, the rod will tip down at the right end, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3942ec65acf89851b3934dedde08467d]

Content:
To balance the rod perfectly, we must move the fulcrum closer to the larger mass.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/8ca82f4e75f06d9a7db1d3718cd02562]

Content:
At what distance from the first mass ([MATH: d_1] in the picture) should the fulcrum be placed for the masses to balance perfectly?

Content:
To answer this, we must introduce the concept of a moment:

Content:
> The moment of a mass about a point [MATH: P] equals the product of the mass and its displacement from [MATH: P.]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- Loosely speaking, moment describes the amount of turning effect produced by a mass about a point (usually the tip of the fulcrum).
- For masses measured in kilograms and distances in meters, the units of a moment are [MATH: \textrm{kg}\cdot\textrm m.]
- Moment is a vector quantity. A moment is either positive (representing clockwise induced motion) or negative (for counterclockwise motion). A moment's sign (positive/clockwise or negative/counterclockwise) is determined by the direction the rod would rotate if the corresponding mass were the only mass in the system.

Content:
Let's now see how to use moments to calculate the required distance [MATH: d_1.]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: The Principle of Moments

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/271f430df6cbf1e7937f02e2552b88ea]

Content:
Let's write down the moment of each mass about the fulcrum:

Content:
- The moment of mass [MATH: A] equals [MATH: -20\cdot d_1 = -20d_1] (negative since the motion induced by this mass would be counterclockwise).
- The moment of mass [MATH: B] equals [MATH: 40\cdot d_2 = 40d_2] (positive since the motion induced by this mass would be clockwise).

Content:
The principle of moments tells us that, for the two masses to balance, the sum of the moments must equal zero.

Content:
So in our case, we have

Content:
[MATH: 40d_2 - 20d_1 = 0.]

Content:
Using the fact that the rod has length [MATH: 1\,\textrm{m},] we have

Content:
[MATH: d_1 + d_2 = 1\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad d_2 = 1 - d_1.]

Content:
Substituting this into the first equation, we get

Content:
[MATH: 40(1-d_1) - 20d_1 = 0]

Content:
which solves to give

Content:
[MATH: d_1 = \dfrac23\,\textrm m.]

Content:
Therefore, if the fulcrum is placed at a distance of [MATH: \dfrac23\,\textrm m] from [MATH: A,] the rod would balance perfectly.

Content:
Before we move on, note the following:

Content:
- The fulcrum also has mass. However, since the distance between the fulcrum and itself is zero, its moment about the fulcrum is zero, and it doesn't feature when we apply the principle of moments. Thus, taking moments about the fulcrum was convenient because we don't need to know its mass! Generally, taking moments about a convenient point can save us a lot of work.
- Selecting a positive sign for a clockwise moment and negative for a counterclockwise moment may seem counterintuitive. After all, positive angles are usually measured counterclockwise. However, we'll soon see that selecting the signs using this convention makes it easy to model moment problems using coordinate axes.

---

Item 3 — Example: Applying the Principle of Moments

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/ce815ce5a9571e39d171d6fccd5e66bf]

Two point masses [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] are connected by a rigid, massless rod of length [MATH: 9\,\rm{ft}] that is perfectly balanced on a fulcrum, as shown above. If [MATH: B] has mass [MATH: 10\,\rm{lb}] and is [MATH: 4\,\rm{ft}] from the fulcrum, find the mass of [MATH: A.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let [MATH: m] be the mass of [MATH: A.]
The length of the rod is [MATH: 9\,\rm{ft}] and the distance between the fulcrum and [MATH: B] is [MATH: 4\,\rm{ft}.] So, the distance between the fulcrum and [MATH: A] is

[MATH: 9 - 4 = 5\,\rm{ft},]

as shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/5fbffe1d0b5c5d2ef8b9c2618163c14b]

Let's write down the moment of each mass about the fulcrum:

- The moment of mass [MATH: A] equals [MATH: -m \cdot 5 = -5m\,\textrm{lb}\cdot\textrm{ft}] (negative since the motion induced by this mass would be counterclockwise).
- The moment of mass [MATH: B] equals [MATH: 10 \cdot 4 = 40\,\textrm{lb}\cdot\textrm{ft}] (positive since the motion induced by this mass would be clockwise).

The principle of moments tells us that for the two masses to balance perfectly, the sum of the moments must equal zero.

Therefore, in this case, we have

[MATH: 40 − 5m|= 0; 5m|= 40; m|= 8lb.]

Item 6 — Tutorial: Moments About the Origin

Content:
As discussed, we denote the direction of a moment as either clockwise or counterclockwise, depending on the direction in which it causes the rod to rotate about the fulcrum.

Content:
In general, the total moment about the origin [MATH: O] of a collection of masses [MATH: m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_n] located at [MATH: x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n] along the [MATH: x]-axis is defined as

Content:
[MATH: M_{O}|= m_{1} ⋅ x_{1} + m_{2} ⋅ x_{2} + ⋯ + m_{n}x_{n}; = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)m_{i}x_{i}.]

Content:
The total moment is a single number that indicates the combined turning effect of the system. A total moment of zero (as in the last example, taking the fulcrum as the origin) means no combined turning effect, so the system balances perfectly.

Content:
The moment of a single mass [MATH: m_i] about the origin is equals [MATH: m_i x_i,] and its sign is determined by its position along the [MATH: x]-axis:

Content:
- If [MATH: x_i > 0,] the induced motion is clockwise, and the associated moment is positive.
- If [MATH: x_i < 0,] the induced motion is counterclockwise, and the associated moment is negative.

Content:
Consider the two point masses below, where the distances along the [MATH: x]-axis are measured in meters. Let's find the total moment of this system about the origin.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/bea90df14c74965d78ecad5e0834b940]

Content:
In this case, we have

Content:
[MATH: m_{1}|= 5,|m_{2}|= 4,; x_{1}|= − 2,|x_{2}|= 3.]

Content:
We calculate the total moment of this system about the origin as follows:

Content:
[MATH: M_{O}|= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)m_{i}x_{i}; = m_{1}x_{1} + m_{2}x_{2}; = 5 ⋅ (− 2) + 4 ⋅ 3; = − 10 + 12; = 2]

Content:
Therefore, the total moment of the system is [MATH: 2\,\textrm{kg} \cdot \textrm{m}.]

Item 7 — Example: Sums of Moments for Masses Distributed Along the X-Axis

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The moment about the origin [MATH: O] of a collection of masses [MATH: m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_n] located at [MATH: x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n] along the [MATH: x]-axis is given by

[MATH: M_O = \sum_{i=1}^n m_i x_i.]

In our case, we have

[MATH: m_{1}|= 1,|m_{2}|= 2,|m_{3}|= 3,|m_{4}|= 3,; x_{1}|= − 1,|x_{2}|= 1,|x_{3}|= 3,|x_{4}|= 5.]

We calculate the total moment of this system about the origin as follows:

[MATH: M_{O}|= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)m_{i}x_{i}; = m_{1}x_{1} + m_{2}x_{2} + m_{3}x_{3} + m_{4}x_{4}; = 1 ⋅ (− 1) + 2 ⋅ 1 + 3 ⋅ 3 + 3 ⋅ 5; = − 1 + 2 + 9 + 15; = 25]

Therefore, the total moment of the system is [MATH: 25\,\textrm{kg} \cdot \textrm{m}.]

Item 10 — Tutorial: Center of Mass

Content:
Suppose we have a collection of masses [MATH: m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_n] located at [MATH: x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n] along the [MATH: x]-axis.

Content:
The system's center of mass is the point [MATH: \bar{x}] on the [MATH: x]-axis where the system's total mass could be concentrated to give the same total moment as the original system.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/32e8140b26cb651550b4b55eed79eaf5]

Content:
Let's derive the equation for the center of mass [MATH: \bar{x}] for this system.

Content:
The total moment of the distributed masses about the origin is given by

Content:
[MATH: M_{O} = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)m_{i}x_{i}.]

Content:
If the total mass of the system is

Content:
[MATH: m = m_1+m_2+\cdots m_n = \sum_{i=1}^n m_i ,]

Content:
then the total moment about the origin of the single mass [MATH: m] located at [MATH: \bar{x}] equals

Content:
[MATH: m \bar{x}.]

Content:
Equating our two moments, we get

Content:
[MATH: M_O = m \bar{x}.]

Content:
Solving for [MATH: \bar{x}], we have

Content:
[MATH: \bar{x} = \dfrac{M_O}{m}.]

Content:
The center of mass is an important physical quantity, as it gives the location where a fulcrum would need to be placed for the system to balance perfectly.
